lines: Cracked handles are small <shake>warnings</shake> with expensive timing.
A dull edge makes every simple job into a bad plan.
A handle should fit the hand, not argue with it.
A sharp edge is useful. A careless one is just trouble with shine.
The bench hears every complaint before the finished tool gets praised.
Cracked handles are warnings. Ignore them and they become stories.
Most days, I am at the smithing table, trying to keep edges and handles from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think toolmaking is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good file more than a loud promise. The file has less to prove.
A good tool saves effort later because someone spent effort first.
Handles teach humility. Ignore the grain and they repay you fast.
Sharp edges are only useful when the rest of the tool is honest.
I judge a tool by how it behaves after a hard day.
Repair work tells you who cared for what they borrowed.
A village needs reliable tools before it can afford grand plans.
Metal and wood argue until the fit is right.
The best tool feels simple because the mistakes were removed.
I trust wear marks more than boasting.
A dull axe turns one problem into several sore ones.
Good work begins with the right tool and continues with better judgment.
There is no shame in repair. Shame is pretending nothing is loose.
A balanced handle keeps anger out of the swing.
The grindstone hears every impatient hand.
Useful things deserve care before they fail.
That time I followed you, the whole plan could have used a better handle.
I remember that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip taught me to ask where we are going before I start walking.
Your plan sounded much safer before we left the village.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the path disappears under us.
I learned to stay close and save my questions for safer ground.
You walk toward danger like it is marked on the route.
Some of those views were worth the sore legs.
If I followed you again, I would bring more food.
The worst stretch was the one you called a shortcut.
I did not expect to miss the sound of the village bell that much.
Every loose stone on that road found the same boot.
I kept wondering whether you knew the way or merely liked the direction.
We made good time whenever nothing chased us.
I was glad to see the rooftops again at the end of it.
That journey taught me which parts of my pack needed better straps.
I would follow you again, but I want the route first.
The road was rough, though your pace kept us moving.
I came home tired and a little less afraid of the world beyond the farms.
A boat is just a tool with a nervous floor. Yours worked, mostly.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It cannot make me forget it.
I spent half the crossing watching the shore and half watching for leaks.
You looked comfortable at the oars. I was busy gripping the seat.
The water was calm until I trusted it.
Next time, tell me how long the crossing is before we push off.
I did not know a boat could creak in so many different ways.
The view was lovely whenever I stopped thinking about the depth.
I would bring a dry cloak if we made that trip again.
Reaching the far bank felt like finishing a difficult repair.
Your boat handled the current better than I expected.
I learned quickly not to stand when the boat turns.
The oars did honest work. My stomach did not.
I kept my tools wrapped tighter than my lunch.
That crossing was faster than the road, though not kinder to my nerves.
I was never so happy to step onto mud.
The spray reached everything I had forgotten to cover.
If we take a boat again, I am sitting in the middle.
We got home dry enough, which is more than I expected.
A tool breaks loudly only after whispering for days.
Good tools make hard work honest. Bad tools make honest work dangerous.
I can fix a cracked handle. A cracked habit takes longer.
Most days, I keep edges and handles from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think toolmaking is simple until something goes wrong.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops.
I trust a good file more than a loud promise.
If you want my honest answer, slow down first.
The village looks calm from a distance. Up close, it is mostly chores and weather.
I notice small flaws. The smithing table trained that into me.
A loose wedge is easier to fix before the axe head flies off.
Use the right tool and half the argument disappears.
I would rather sharpen a blade twice than replace a careless finger.
Oak makes a sturdy handle, but only if the grain runs true.
Rust is patient. That is why cleaning cannot be.
Balance matters more than weight when a tool stays in your hand all day.
If a hinge squeaks, it is already asking for oil.
A repair should outlast the excuse that brought it to my bench.
You can tell who lends tools by how many names are scratched into the handles.
The cheapest fix is usually the one done before anything snaps.
